newsitem.title: USA: Pentagon gay policy not "dismal failure" - Cohen.
newsitem.headline: Pentagon gay policy not "dismal failure" - Cohen.

text.p: Defence Secretary William Cohen on Wednesday denied that a Pentagon policy protecting homosexuals in uniform was a failure despite charges that an increasing number of gays and lesbians are being discharged.

"I don't think you can call it a dismal failure," Cohen said while vowing to uphold the three-year-old policy allowing homosexuals to serve without fear of witch hunts or prosecution if they remain silent on their sexual orientation.

A study by the Servicemembers Legal Defence Network, an aid organisation for those in the military accused of homosexuality, charged this week that more men and women are now being discharged for homosexuality than before the controversial policy went into effect in 1994.
The study said 850 men and women were discharged from the military for homosexuality in the year ending this month, an 18 percent increase from the previous year and a 42 percent increase from 1994.

Cohen told reporters during a Pentagon photo opportunity with visiting Saudi Defence Minister Prince Sultan that he had not examined the study in detail but saw no reason now to change the policy to crack down on perceived harassment of homosexuals.

Under the "Don't ask, don't tell, don't pursue" policy, homosexuals in the U.S. military are supposed to be protected from active investigation and dismissal as long as they remain silent on the issue.
"I have not had a chance to fully review the report. My understanding is that there are fluctuations up and down during the course of any given year dealing with this policy," Cohen said.
"So it's a problem that we are looking at, but it is not of such a gravity as would warrant any change of policy from my perspective at this point," he added.
"We are always going to enforce the policy. If I find that the policy is being violated, that there is active pursuit and prosecution, I will do whatever I can to see that that's stopped."
On taking office in January 1993, President Bill Clinton at first tried to impose a flat rule prohibiting discrimination against homosexuals in the military.
But a compromise was made in 1994 after fierce opposition from senior leaders in the military and conservative members of Congress.
